o: Parse left to right; at each position try to match one of the ten digit words (lengths 3–5); on a match emit the digit and jump past it, otherwise skip one character. Since only ten fixed words exist, checking substrings of length 3, 4, 5 against a hash set is O(len(s)) overall. A trie is the scalable alternative but unnecessary at this size.
k: All digit words have length 3–5, so at most three substring checks per position suffice.

a.i: Map each word to its digit; at each index test the 3-, 4-, and 5-character prefixes.
s: i = 0; while i < len(s): try lengths 5,4,3 (or 3..5); on match append digit, i += len; else i += 1.
Join digits into the answer string.

a.i: Insert all ten words into a trie; at each position walk the trie as far as characters match, emitting a digit if a terminal node is reached. Avoids substring hashing and scales to large dictionaries.
s: Build trie of the ten words with digit markers at terminals.
At each index, walk children while they exist; record the digit if a terminal is hit.
Advance past the longest match, else skip one char.

w: The hash-set version is the interview default; mention the trie for follow-ups with big dictionaries or streaming input. Pitfall: forgetting partial matches like "tw" must consume characters one at a time (the skip-one rule), and "zeero" must yield empty. Follow-up: overlapping encodings where greedy longest match matters.
